w: Its near-symmetric pyramid rises 4,478 m over Zermatt, one of the most photographed summits on earth. Three of its four faces sit on the Swiss side; the south face looks down on Breuil-Cervinia in Italy. Just east, the Theodul Pass has carried trade between the valleys since Roman times.
s: The 'Mountain of Mountains' towering over Zermatt
_facts: 4,478m; described as the most photographed mountain in the world
South face overlooks Breuil-Cervinia, Italy; other three faces Swiss
Theodul Pass to its east has been a trade route since Roman times
Studied by Horace-Benedict de Saussure in the late 18th century

w: Its highest point, the Dufourspitze at 4,634 m, is the second-highest summit in the Alps after Mont Blanc and the tallest in Switzerland. The massif spans four faces across Italy and Switzerland; the north-western one drains toward the Mattertal and Zermatt via one of the Alps' largest glaciers.
s: Switzerland's roof, feeding Zermatt's biggest glacier
_facts: Dufourspitze, 4,634m, is the massif's highest point
Second-highest summit in the Alps after Mont Blanc
North-west face feeds one of the Alps' largest glaciers, above Zermatt

w: Named for the surveyor Guillaume-Henri Dufour, this 4,634 m summit is the highest point in Switzerland and the second-highest in the Alps after Mont Blanc. A party of eight, led by guides Matthaus and Johannes Zumtaugwald and Ulrich Lauener, reached the top from Zermatt on 1 August 1855, Switzerland's National Day.
s: Reached on Swiss National Day, 1855, from Zermatt
_facts: 4,634m; highest point in Switzerland
Named after surveyor Guillaume-Henri Dufour
First reached 1 Aug 1855 from Zermatt, on Swiss National Day, by a party of eight

a: between the Anniviers and Zermatt valleys
w: At 4,505 m, its pyramidal shape and pure white slopes lead many mountaineers to call it the most beautiful mountain in the Alps. The Irish physicist John Tyndall made the first ascent from Randa in 1861 with guides J.J. Bennen and Ulrich Wenger. In 1991 two rockslides tore off a cliff above Randa.
s: The 'white peak' many call the Alps' most beautiful
_facts: First climbed 1861 by John Tyndall with guides J.J. Bennen and Ulrich Wenger, from Randa
1991: two rockslides above Randa on its east side

w: Named with its neighbour Pollux after the Gemini twins, Castor is the higher of the pair at 4,225 m, between the Breithorn and Monte Rosa. A 3,847 m pass, the Zwillingsjoch, separates the two. The first ascent came on 23 August 1861, usually climbed from the Capanna Quintino Sella hut on the Italian side.
s: Twin peak named for the Gemini, first climbed 1861
_facts: 4,225m; named with neighbour Pollux for the Gemini twins
Separated from Pollux by the Zwillingsjoch pass, 3,847m
First ascent 23 August 1861

w: At 4,327 m, three ridges meet at a sharp point that gives the mountain its name - Nadel is German for needle. It is the highest summit on the Nadelgrat, the ridge above Saas-Fee to the east and the Mattertal to the west. Four guides made the first ascent on 16 September 1858.
s: The 'needle peak' of the Nadelgrat, climbed since 1858
_facts: 4,327m; highest point on the Nadelgrat ridge
Name means 'needle' in German, from its sharp-pointed summit
First climbed 16 Sept 1858 by Andenmatten, Epiney, Supersaxo and Zimmermann

a: above Zermatt, over the Gorner Glacier
w: The Gornergrat rack railway climbs to this 3,135 m rocky ridge above Zermatt, overlooking the Gorner Glacier: it is the highest open-air railway in Europe. Near the summit sits the Kulm Hotel at 3,120 m; in the late 1960s two astronomical observatories were built into its towers.
s: Europe's highest open-air railway, with observatories on top
_facts: 3,135m ridge overlooking the Gorner Glacier
Reached by the Gornergrat rack railway, the highest open-air railway in Europe
Kulm Hotel at 3,120m has hosted astronomical observatories since the late 1960s

w: The Dom, at 4,546 m, is the main summit of this massif, the seventh-highest peak in the Alps by height but third by prominence. Its normal route gains more vertical height than any other alpine 4000er, none by mechanical means. The name Mischabel comes from a dialect word for pitchfork.
s: The 'pitchfork' massif crowned by the Dom
_facts: Dom (4,546m) is the massif's main summit, 7th-highest in the Alps by height
By prominence, 3rd-highest in the Alps and 2nd in Switzerland
'Mischabel' derives from a dialect word for pitchfork
Dom named for Canon Berchtold of Sitten cathedral, its first surveyor

w: Its two summits, the main peak at 3,669 m and a north-top at 3,659 m, give the mountain its name: Besso means 'twins' in the local Val d'Anniviers dialect. Guides likely made the first ascent in 1862. The classic south-west ridge route is nicknamed the 'Ladies' Route'.
_facts: Two summits: 3,669m main peak, 3,659m north-top
Name means 'twins' in the local Val d'Anniviers dialect
First ascent probably 1862 by guides Epinay and Vianin
Classic south-west ridge route nicknamed the 'Ladies' Route'
